title: Soil chemistry

definition.text: The study of the chemical characteristics of soil.

facts.text: A soil's chemistry depends on its mineral composition, its organic matter and environmental factors.
J. Thomas Way, consulting chemist to the Royal Agricultural Society of England, ran many experiments on how soils exchange ions in the early 1870s and is considered the father of soil chemistry.
Until the late 1960s the field focused on reactions behind soil formation and plant growth; concern over pollution then shifted its emphasis toward environmental soil science.
Minerals, derived from the parent rock or regolith, make up about 90% of the total weight of soil.
Plants take part by exchanging nutrients with microorganisms and absorbing nutrients, which creates concentration gradients of cations and anions in the soil.
Plant nutrients follow their own biogeochemical cycles: nitrogen passes from a gas into nitrate and nitrite, while phosphorus moves in mineral form held in rock.
Agricultural soil science applies soil chemistry mainly to plant nutrients, soil fertility and fertilizer components.

notes: Part overview page for Soil chemistry. Its Key concepts sections (soil structure, texture, biota, soil air, cycles) repeat material owned by other chapters and were not drafted here.

definition.text: The part of soil chemistry that studies how contaminants are released into soil and what becomes of them there.

facts.text: Once a chemical reaches soil, adsorption and desorption, precipitation, polymerization, dissolution, hydrolysis, hydration, complexation and oxidation–reduction can raise or lower its toxicity.
Knowing these reactions helps predict a contaminant's fate and toxicity and design sound, cost-effective clean-up, though remediation engineers often disregard them.
Worry about pollution and ecological and health risks since the late 1960s turned soil chemistry from pedology and farming toward environmental soil science.

definition.text: The laboratory techniques soil chemists use to study reactions in samples taken from undisturbed horizons, run with replicated treatments and controls.

facts.text: Air-drying samples at about 25 °C and sieving them to 2 mm markedly disrupts structure, microbial diversity and pH- and redox-related properties, so many chemists now keep samples field-moist at 4 °C.
In batch equilibration a solution of known ion content is shaken with soil, for example 25 mL with 5 g, then separated and analysed to give mg of ion per g of soil.
Column studies leach a solution through soil at a controlled rate to mimic rain, snowmelt and irrigation water passing through a field.
In situ surface spectroscopy, such as infrared, NMR, Mössbauer and X-ray methods, shows how ions bind to particle and colloid surfaces without disturbing the soil.

title: Clay mineral

definition.text: A hydrous aluminium phyllosilicate: a sheet-structured silicate that may also carry iron, magnesium, alkali metals and other cations.

facts.text: Clay minerals form in the presence of water, as common products of weathering, including weathering of feldspar, and of low-temperature hydrothermal alteration.
They are very common in soils and in fine-grained rocks such as shale, mudstone, siltstone, slate and phyllite.
Their structure rests on flat hexagonal sheets like those of the mica minerals.
Clay's ability to hold nutrient cations such as potassium and ammonium matters for soil fertility; cation exchange capacity comes mainly from charges on clay minerals and organic matter.
Clay minerals keep forming for as long as a soil exists, by inheritance, by neoformation or by transformation of earlier minerals.
Most soil clays are crystalline, but some are amorphous; a soil's clay is a mixture of types, with one often dominating according to soil type.
Only with X-ray diffraction in the 1930s did clay prove to be mainly sheet silicates formed as secondary minerals, not tiny grains of quartz, feldspar or mica.
Because they need water to form, clay minerals are rare in the Solar System, though they have been detected on Mars, Ceres and other bodies.

title: Tetrahedral and octahedral sheets

definition.text: The two kinds of sheet that build every clay mineral: one of corner-sharing silica tetrahedra, and one of small cations such as aluminium or magnesium each surrounded by six oxygens.

facts.text: In a tetrahedral sheet each tetrahedron shares three oxygens with its neighbours in a hexagonal array; the fourth, apical oxygen points the same way on every tetrahedron.
The apical oxygens also form one face of the octahedral sheet, and an extra oxygen above each hexagonal gap bonds to hydrogen as a hydroxyl group.
Kaolinite shows the naming: its T sheet holds silicon among four oxygens, its O sheet aluminium among six oxygens or hydroxyls.
Fitting the two sheets together corrugates the tetrahedral sheet and flattens the octahedral one.
Depending on composition, a layer is neutral or carries a net negative charge, balanced by interlayer cations such as Na+ or K+ or by a lone octahedral sheet.
A clay crystal is a stack of these layers separated by interlayers.

title: 1:1 and 2:1 clay minerals

definition.text: The basic division of clay minerals by how their sheets stack: one tetrahedral and one octahedral sheet per layer in 1:1 clays, an octahedral sheet between two tetrahedral sheets in 2:1 clays.

facts.text: Kaolinite and serpentine are 1:1 clays; talc, vermiculite and montmorillonite are 2:1 clays.
1:1 layers are uncharged and held by hydrogen bonds; 2:1 layers carry a net negative charge and are bound by cations, as in illite and smectites, or by octahedral sheets, as in chlorites.
The main groups are kaolin (kaolinite, dickite, halloysite, nacrite), smectite (montmorillonite, nontronite, beidellite, saponite), illite and chlorite.
Palygorskite and sepiolite are 2:1 clays with long water channels inside their structure.
Mixed-layer clays interleave two types, randomly (R0) or in order; perfectly ordered R1 illite–smectite is called rectorite and chlorite–smectite corrensite.
In soils, the four main groups are usually given as kaolinite, montmorillonite–smectite, illite and chlorite.

title: Clay mineral identification
article: Clay mineral#Tests which verify that clay minerals are present

definition.text: Laboratory tests that confirm and quantify clay minerals, using glycol adsorption, cation exchange capacity, X-ray diffraction, differential thermal analysis and chemical analysis.

facts.text: Clay minerals are usually too fine for ordinary optical study, so X-ray diffraction is the main tool, aided by electron diffraction, spectroscopy and SEM-EDS.
Once organic matter, carbonates, free oxides and non-clay minerals are measured, clay percentages are estimated from glycol adsorption, CEC, K2O and thermal data.
Illite is estimated from potassium oxide content, since it is the only clay mineral containing potassium.
Glycol adsorption measures how much ethylene glycol enters a clay's interlayer sites when it is exposed to the vapour at 60 °C for eight hours.

title: Clay hypothesis of the origin of life
article: Clay mineral#Clay and the origins of life

definition.text: The idea, proposed by Graham Cairns-Smith in 1985, that complex organic molecules arose on non-organic, replicating silicate crystal surfaces in water.

facts.text: Montmorillonite has been shown to catalyse the joining of nucleotides into RNA in water, and the formation of membranes from lipids.
In 1998 Hyman Hartman proposed that the first organisms were self-replicating iron-rich clays that fixed carbon dioxide into oxalic and other dicarboxylic acids.
Clay minerals form only where water is present, and many theories of abiogenesis involve them.

notes: Origin-of-life science rather than soil science; drafted because it is its own section on a seed page.

title: Soil colloids

definition.text: The microscopically small particles in soil, chiefly clay and humus, whose charged surfaces hold and exchange ions with the soil water.

facts.text: Colloidal particles have at least one dimension between about 1 nm and 1 μm.
High specific surface area and unbalanced negative charges make clay, a colloidal and usually crystalline phyllosilicate, the most active mineral part of soil.
Negative charges on colloids hold cations and positive charges hold anions, giving soil its cation and anion exchange capacities.
Exchange between colloids and soil water buffers soil pH, alters structure and purifies percolating water by adsorbing cations, useful and harmful.
Soil clays fall into layered alumino-silica clays, crystalline chain carbonates and sulfates, young amorphous clays, and old, highly leached sesquioxide clays.
Humus forms the organic colloids; on a dry-weight basis its CEC is many times that of clay.
Heat and heavy rain in tropical rainforests largely destroy clay and organic colloids, leaving only sesquioxide clays of low CEC.

notes: No Soil colloid article crawled; anchored on Soil matrix (a Density, pores and compaction seed) because its colloid sections are the subject's only systematic treatment. Check overlap with that chapter's Soil matrix entry.

title: Isomorphous substitution

definition.text: The replacement, while a clay forms, of cations in its crystal structure by others of lower valence, which leaves the clay a permanent negative charge.

facts.text: Al3+ may replace Si4+ in the silica sheet, and up to a quarter of the Al3+ in the alumina sheet may be replaced by Zn2+, Mg2+ or Fe2+.
Swapping Al(III) for Si(IV) turns a balanced +4/−4 site into +3/−4, a charge of −1; Mg2+ for Al3+ in the octahedral sheet gives +2/−3, also −1.
The excess negative charge must be balanced by cations in the interlayer, and it attracts water and positively charged cations, some useful to plants.
Substitutions in outer layers count for more than inner ones, since charge strength falls off with the square of the distance.
Montmorillonite's charge is mostly octahedral, from Mg replacing Al; beidellite's is mostly tetrahedral, from Al replacing Si.
Kaolinite has undergone almost no substitution, which is why its CEC is low.
This charge forms with the clay and does not change with time, unlike pH-dependent charge, which rises as pH rises.

notes: No crawled article; passes the 2+ pages test (Soil, Soil matrix, Smectite, Montmorillonite). The Charge and nutrient holding chapter may draft permanent charge from Soil#Cation and anion exchange: merge if so.

title: Clay mineral weathering sequence

definition.text: The change in a soil's dominant clay minerals as weathering and leaching intensify, from 2:1 clays such as montmorillonite through kaolinite to iron and aluminium oxides.

facts.text: The clay that forms depends on the parent material and on the minerals in solution, so source rock and climate both matter.
Montmorillonite occurs in soils that have had little leaching, hence in arid regions, though depending on its origin it may occur in humid climates.
Where rainfall is high, acid soils lose more silica than alumina from their clays, leaving kaolinite; heavier weathering still produces sesquioxide clays.
Kaolinite abounds in soils of hot, moist climates; along gradients toward cooler climates illite increases, and toward drier ones smectite.
Acid weathering of feldspar-rich rock in warm climates yields kaolin, alkaline weathering yields illite, and intense weathering of other clay minerals yields gibbsite.
Because clay content tracks climate, the clays of buried ancient soils are used to infer past climates.

notes: No article; sentences on Soil matrix, Kaolinite and Clay#Formation. May overlap a Clay#Formation entry in What soil is made of.

title: Chlorite (clay mineral)

definition.text: A chemically varied group of 2:1 clay minerals whose layers are bound by a positively charged hydrated magnesium sheet.

facts.text: Its 2:1 layers carry negative charge from aluminium replacing silicon and are bound by positively charged hydroxide (brucite) sheets, not by scattered cations as in vermiculite or mica.
With two silicon planes, one aluminium and one magnesium plane, it is described as a 2:2 clay.
Water is not adsorbed between its layers, so chlorite does not swell, and its CEC is low.
A common weathering product found widely in clay, it also forms in low-grade metamorphic rocks; the name is Greek for green, and it contains no chlorine.

notes: Gap-fill: article set to the Chlorite group page; earlier sentences from Clay mineral and Soil matrix kept.

definition.text: A common 1:1 clay mineral with the composition Al2Si2O5(OH)4, also called kaolin.

facts.text: It is a soft, earthy, usually white mineral produced by chemical weathering of aluminium silicate minerals such as feldspar.
Each layer bonds a silica tetrahedral sheet to an aluminium octahedral sheet, and successive layers are held together by hydrogen bonds.
Its layers carry no net charge, so no large cations sit between them, which explains its low cation exchange capacity of 1–15 meq/100 g.
Tight hydrogen bonding keeps water from entering between the layers, so kaolinite does not swell and has a low shrink–swell capacity.
When moist, a film of water binds its plate-like crystals yet lets them slip, making the clay plastic; dried it is rigid but fragile, and plastic again when rewetted.
Kaolinite surfaces, like those of allophane and iron and aluminium oxides, often carry positive charges.
It abounds in soils formed by chemical weathering in hot, moist climates; soils whose clay is mostly kaolinite are called kaolisols in the INERA classification.
Rock rich in kaolinite is kaolin or china clay, an industrial raw material used above all for paper and ceramics.

definition.text: The crystallization of kaolinite from silica and aluminium in solution at ordinary temperature and pressure, as happens in soils.

facts.text: In soils, disordered amorphous material seems to turn into ordered kaolinite fairly quickly, at ambient temperature and pressure and without major environmental change.
Silica must arrive as single molecules in very dilute solution, and aluminium must be six-coordinated with oxygen, as in gibbsite.
In the reaction 2Al(OH)3 + 2H4SiO4 → Si2O5·Al2(OH)4 + 5H2O, five water molecules must be removed for each unit of kaolinite formed.
On basalt in Kivu, kaolinite formed only where wet and dry seasons alternate, not in perennially swampy ground; wetting–drying cycles also help allophane turn into kaolinite.

title: Halloysite

definition.text: An aluminosilicate clay mineral of the kaolinite group, with the formula Al2Si2O5(OH)4.

facts.text: It occurs mainly in recently exposed volcanic soils but also forms from primary minerals in tropical soils; glassy basaltic rocks alter to it most readily.
It grows as nanotubes with walls 10–15 sheets thick, outer diameters of 50–60 nm and lengths of 0.5–10 μm.
Hydrated halloysite has a layer spacing of 1 nm and dehydrated meta-halloysite 0.7 nm; its CEC rises with hydration, from 5–10 to 40–50 meq/100 g.
Allophane alters to halloysite under resilicating conditions, and montmorillonite alters to its hydrated form, endellite, in acidic cave settings at pH 5 or lower.

notes: Assigned to no chapter; own crawled article and mentioned on Clay mineral, Allophane and Montmorillonite.

title: Smectite

definition.text: A group of swelling 2:1 clay minerals, mainly montmorillonite, that take water and cations between their layers.

facts.text: Smectite and montmorillonite name the same class of swelling clays, smectite being the usual term in Europe and montmorillonite in North America; industry calls them bentonite.
Each layer is two silica tetrahedral sheets cross-linked through an octahedral sheet of alumina or iron oxide.
The layers are not rigidly joined: the interlayer between them holds hydrated cations and water, and smectite swells as water and cations enter it reversibly.
Its layers are negatively charged by isomorphous substitution in both the tetrahedral and the octahedral sheets.
Because the interlayer is open to water and cations, smectites have the highest CEC of the clays common in soils; only vermiculite and some zeolites exceed it.
Smectites form by weathering of basalt, gabbro and silica-rich volcanic glass, and where hot water or seawater dissolves much of the silica from volcanic ash.
Soils with smectite clay expand when wet, and clay soils containing montmorillonite or smectite suffer alkalinity problems more than illite or kaolinite clay soils.

notes: Expansive clay's lead (S:659fc42212a9) lists kaolinite and illite among smectite minerals, which looks garbled; not used.

title: Interlayer cations and clay swelling
article: Smectite#Role of interlayer cations in the swelling process

definition.text: How the cations held between the layers of 2:1 clays govern how much the clay swells or shrinks as it gains or loses water.

facts.text: Na+ and Ca2+ are the main interlayer cations in smectites; sodium gives the most swelling, while calcium smectite swells much less but also shrinks less when dried.
How strongly each cation hydrates, and its hydrated radius, explain the swelling or shrinking of layered silicates.
Highly hydrated magnesium ions act as swellers, fully opening vermiculite's interlayer; poorly hydrated potassium ions act as collapsers, fully closing illite's.
Potassium replacing sodium collapses the interlayer, so smectite in contact with potassium-rich groundwater turns into non-swelling illite.
With sodium as its main exchangeable cation, montmorillonite can swell to several times its original volume.
Ammonium is fixed mainly between the layers of 2:1 clays such as illite, vermiculite or montmorillonite, along with ions of similar size and low hydration energy such as potassium.

title: Montmorillonite

definition.text: A soft 2:1 clay mineral of the smectite group, with an alumina sheet between two silica sheets and a water content that varies.

facts.text: It is named after Montmorillon in France, where it was first described in 1847.
Its plate-shaped particles average about 1 μm across and 0.96 nm thick; resolving one takes about 25,000-fold electron-microscope magnification.
Its CEC comes from magnesium replacing aluminium in the central sheet, which leaves nearby oxygens negatively charged and able to attract cations.
Its crystals are loosely bound, so water enters between them and the clay can swell up to ten times its dry volume; it is a characteristic component of swelling soils.
Because its crystals are not bonded face to face, its whole surface is open to reactions, giving it a high CEC.
It occurs in soils that have had little leaching, hence in arid regions, often mixed with chlorite, muscovite, illite and kaolinite.
It is added to drought-prone soils to hold water, and its swelling suits it to drilling mud, earthen dams and levees.

notes: Swelling figures differ by material: montmorillonite up to ten times its dry volume (Soil matrix, S:6875f76bfb72), several times with sodium (S:7613fd1e2a50); bentonite rock up to a factor of eight (S:99eec84cfa5d).

definition.text: A group of closely related, non-expanding 2:1 clay minerals, also called hydromica, structurally close to muscovite.

facts.text: Poorly hydrated potassium ions fill the space between its layers and bind them strongly, so illite does not swell.
Compared with muscovite it holds slightly more silicon, magnesium, iron and water and slightly less tetrahedral aluminium and interlayer potassium.
Its CEC, typically 20–30 meq/100 g, is lower than smectite's but higher than kaolinite's.
It forms by alteration of muscovite and feldspar in weathering and hydrothermal settings, and from smectite exposed to potassium-rich groundwater.
Illite is common in sediments, soils and argillaceous rocks, and its share of soil clay rises relative to kaolinite toward cooler climates.
Potassium bonds shrink its active surface, and how much it swells depends on how far potassium feldspar has weathered.
Its tiny crystals usually need X-ray diffraction or SEM-EDS to identify, and it is the only clay mineral containing potassium.
It was first described in 1937 from the Maquoketa shale of Calhoun County, Illinois, and named after the state.

definition.text: A hydrous 2:1 phyllosilicate clay mineral that expands greatly when heated.

facts.text: It forms by weathering or hydrothermal alteration of biotite or phlogopite: these micas lose the potassium between their sheets, which is replaced by magnesium and iron.
It is a limited-expansion clay with a medium shrink–swell capacity: hydrated magnesium holds its crystals loosely, so it swells, but less than montmorillonite.
Its cation exchange capacity of 100–150 meq/100 g is high, above that of smectite.
Heating makes it exfoliate, which gave it its name, from the Latin vermiculare, 'to breed worms'; it was first described in 1824 at Millbury, Massachusetts.
It occurs interlayered with chlorite, biotite and phlogopite, typically where felsic rocks meet mafic or ultramafic ones.
Pure vermiculite contains no asbestos, but ore from some deposits, notably the Libby mine in Montana, was contaminated, and some products contained asbestos until the early 1990s.

definition.text: The use of heat-expanded vermiculite in potting mixes, seed raising and garden soils to hold water, air and nutrients for plants.

facts.text: Mixed with peat or composted pine bark, exfoliated vermiculite makes soilless growing media that speed root growth and hold air, fertilizer and moisture for release as plants need them.
Alone or mixed with soil or peat, it is used to germinate seeds with very little watering.
In heavy, sticky soils, mixing in vermiculite up to half the soil's volume creates air channels; in sandy soils it helps the soil hold water and air.
Agromineral practice uses vermiculites and zeolites to store moisture in soil, alongside perlite for aeration.

title: Allophane

definition.text: An amorphous to poorly crystalline hydrous aluminium silicate clay mineraloid.

facts.text: It has only short-range order, so it is a mineraloid; it forms from weathering or hydrothermal alteration of volcanic glass and feldspars, typically at pH 5–7, with an Al:Si ratio usually of 2.
Electron micrographs show aggregates of hollow spherules about 3–5 nm across, built from curved alumina and silica layers.
It alters to halloysite where silica is added and to gibbsite where silica is removed.
With imogolite and ferrihydrite it is among the amorphous colloidal materials that define Andisols, soils formed in volcanic ash.

contested_note: The source says allophane's structure has been debated, though it describes curved alumina and silica layers similar to clay minerals.

definition.text: An aluminium silicate clay mineral, Al2SiO3(OH)4, made of a network of tiny nanotubes.

facts.text: It occurs in soils formed from volcanic ash; first described in 1962 in Kumamoto prefecture, Japan, it is named from imogo, a brownish-yellow soil derived from volcanic ash.
Its tubes are about 2 nm across outside and 1 nm inside, with walls of gibbsite sheets and orthosilicate groups.
It occurs together with allophane, quartz, cristobalite, gibbsite, vermiculite and limonite.
Where tephra is basic or the climate dry, allophane and imogolite develop and Andosols receive the Silandic qualifier.

title: Amorphous clays

definition.text: Young mixtures of silica and alumina in soil that have not yet had time to form regular crystals.

facts.text: They are common in recent volcanic ash deposits such as tephra.
Most of their charge comes from hydroxyl groups that gain or lose a hydrogen ion as soil pH changes, so they buffer soil pH and can attract cations or anions.
Andisols are defined by high proportions of glass and amorphous colloidal materials, including allophane, imogolite and ferrihydrite.
Clays without plate-shaped minerals, such as allophanic clays, tend not to show a residual shear strength.

notes: S:739d81b6d204 says a hydroxyl that loses its hydrogen shows a positive charge, and S:d55c0d0e910d gives high CEC in acid and high anion exchange in basic solution; both look inverted, so neither direction is stated. definition.text: An absorbent swelling clay made mostly of montmorillonite, in either its sodium or its calcium form.

facts.text: Geologists use the name for a clay rock formed from volcanic ash, usually in seawater, as up to 40–50 wt.% of its silica dissolves away; industry uses it for any smectite-rich swelling clay.
It can absorb enough water to grow up to eight times in volume, and sodium bentonite swells far more than calcium bentonite.
Calcium bentonite can be turned into sodium bentonite by ion exchange, by mixing in 5–10% of a soluble sodium salt such as sodium carbonate.
Swelling makes sodium bentonite a self-sealing, low-permeability barrier: it lines landfills, and nearly sodium-saturated clay forms impermeable curtains in soil below dams.

definition.text: Adding bentonite clay to degraded farm soils to restore them, as farmers in northeast Thailand have done.

facts.text: In northeast Thailand, bentonite applied to degraded soils dramatically reversed the degradation and brought higher yields, better crop prices and greater returns.
Field trials by the International Water Management Institute and partners in 2002–2003 found that locally sourced bentonite raised yields of rain-fed forage sorghum.
Clay-using farmers had higher costs, but larger, better harvests let them invest and grow more than farmers who did not use clay.
Adding clays such as calcium bentonite to water-repellent soils gives them more surface area per unit volume and supports aggregation.

title: Fuller's earth

definition.text: Any of various clays used as an absorbent, filter or bleaching agent.

facts.text: Products sold as fuller's earth are usually palygorskite (attapulgite) or bentonite; its clays commonly include montmorillonite, kaolinite and attapulgite.
In some places the name means calcium bentonite, altered volcanic ash made mostly of montmorillonite.
The name comes from fulling: fullers kneaded it with water into woollen cloth to absorb lanolin, oils and other greasy impurities.
Saturated by heavy rain it can become thixotropic, so hills, cliffs and slopes that contain it can be unstable.

notes: Industrial, cosmetic and film uses skipped; the debated health concern (S:265a680660ac) is about its use as film dust, not soils.

title: Clay–water interaction

definition.text: The umbrella term for the progressive interactions between clay minerals and water, described in five stages: hydration, dispersion, flocculation, deflocculation and aggregation.

facts.text: Dry clay packets sit in face-to-face stacks like a deck of playing cards; in water they first hydrate, absorbing water and swelling.
In dispersion, water pushes the platelets so far apart that they lose their attraction and spread through the water; once shearing stops, surface charges draw them back together in flocculation.
Deflocculation, or peptization, reverses flocculation: a chemical deflocculant covers the platelets' positive edge charges and greatly weakens their attraction.
Aggregation, driven by ionic or thermal conditions, alters the water layer around the platelets, strips deflocculant from their edges and lets them return to face-to-face stacking.

notes: Short seed page (7 sentences, no inlinks). The pilot's Flocculation and Soil dispersion entries cover the soil-structure side; this entry is the clay-mineral sequence.

definition.text: An iron(III) oxide-hydroxide mineral, the α form of FeO(OH), found in soils and other low-temperature settings such as sediment.

facts.text: It often forms by weathering of other iron-rich minerals, so it is a common soil component, concentrated in laterites, which consist of kaolinite, quartz, hematite and goethite.

Its formation turns ferrous into ferric iron: as iron-bearing minerals reach the soil's oxidation zone, iron(II) becomes iron(III) while the parent mineral's shape is kept, so goethite often forms pseudomorphs.
It is the main component of rust and of bog iron ore, which forms in swampy ground at the head of springs.
Goethite is yellowish to reddish to dark brown or black; soils rich in sesquioxides range from yellow to red according to their dominant iron oxides.
Clays rich in goethite hold phosphorus so tightly that plants cannot absorb it.
Heating converts goethite and ferrihydrite to maghemite, which raises soil magnetism.
Some bacteria produce goethite through their excretion processes.
Long used as the pigment brown ochre, it was first described in 1806 and named after Johann Wolfgang von Goethe.

title: Gibbsite

definition.text: A mineral form of aluminium hydroxide, Al(OH)3.

facts.text: It is built of stacked sheets of linked octahedra, each an aluminium ion bonded to six hydroxide groups, with a third of the octahedral sites left empty.
Each sheet is electrically neutral, so no ions glue the sheets together; only weak residual bonds do, which makes gibbsite very soft and easily cleaved.
Identical aluminium hydroxide 'gibbsite layers' are sandwiched between silicate sheets in the illite, kaolinite and smectite clay groups.
Gibbsite forms by intense weathering of other clay minerals, and allophane alters to it where silica is removed.
It is among the less soluble oxides left when heavy rainfall leaches most silica from alumino-silica clays, as in the lateritic weathering profiles of tropical soils.
As one of the three main phases of bauxite, it is an important aluminium ore.
It is named after the American mineral collector George Gibbs (1776–1833).

notes: S:ff033ea6352e carries a citation-needed tag.

title: Sesquioxide clays

definition.text: Old, highly leached soil clays made of oxides and hydroxides of iron, aluminium and titanium, left after heavy rainfall removes most of the silica from alumino-silica clays.

facts.text: They include hematite (Fe2O3), iron hydroxide (Fe(OH)3), gibbsite (Al(OH)3) and the manganese mineral birnessite, as seen in lateritic weathering profiles of tropical soils.
Forming them takes hundreds of thousands of years of leaching.
Their name comes from the Latin sesqui, 'one and one-half', for three parts oxygen to two of iron or aluminium, a ratio that does not hold for them all.
They are not sticky and do not swell; soils rich in them, such as lateritic soils, behave much like sand and pass water rapidly.
Their CEC is low, but as variable-charge minerals they can hold anions as well as cations.
They hold large amounts of phosphate, a sorption that humified organic matter partly inhibits; the more goethite they contain, the more phosphorus is locked away from plants.
Soils rich in them range from yellow to red according to which iron oxides dominate.
In tropical rainforests heavy rains wash the alumino-silicate clays out of the soil, leaving only sesquioxide clays of low CEC.

title: Diatomaceous earth

definition.text: A soft, siliceous sedimentary rock, also called diatomite or kieselgur, that crumbles into a fine white to off-white powder.

facts.text: It consists of the fossilized silica shells of diatoms accumulated in lake or marine sediments over millions of years, and is usually 80–90% silica.
Its particles are typically 10 to 200 μm, and its high porosity gives the powder a low density.
In FAO soil description, siliceous diatomaceous earth is one of the materials of limnic L layers, alongside coprogenous earth and marl.
Gardeners use it as a soil conditioner and bonsai medium because, like perlite and vermiculite, it holds water and nutrients yet drains freely and keeps the medium aerated.

title: Bauxite

definition.text: A sedimentary rock with a relatively high aluminium content, the world's main source of aluminium.

facts.text: It consists mostly of the aluminium minerals gibbsite, boehmite and diaspore, mixed with goethite, hematite, kaolinite and small amounts of anatase.
Lateritic bauxites, found mostly in the tropics, form by lateritization of silicate rocks such as granite, gneiss, basalt and shale; karst bauxites lie over limestone and dolomite.

Even more than iron-rich laterites, bauxite needs intense weathering and very good drainage, which dissolve kaolinite and precipitate gibbsite, almost the only aluminium hydroxide in lateritic bauxites.
Most deposits lie within 1 to 20 metres of the surface, so bauxite is usually strip mined, with little or no overburden.

notes: Assigned page. Aluminium and gallium production, maritime safety and mining conflicts skipped.

title: Fougèrite

definition.text: A naturally occurring green rust mineral, a layered double hydroxide of ferrous and ferric iron, described only relatively recently.

facts.text: It was first found in forest soils near Fougères, Brittany, and accepted as a mineral species by the International Mineralogical Association in 2002.
Its brucite-like layers hold Fe2+ and Fe3+, with loosely bound carbonate and water between them, and it forms clay-like hexagonal platelets under a micron across.
Green rust occurs as the mineral fougèrite in Gleysols.
Unstable in air, it oxidizes, dehydrates and loses carbonate, turning to ferrihydrite and finally to lepidocrocite or goethite.

notes: Assigned page.

title: Palygorskite

definition.text: A fibrous magnesium aluminium clay mineral, also called attapulgite, with the formula (Mg,Al)2Si4O10(OH)·4(H2O).

facts.text: Unlike layered smectites it has a ribbon structure of continuous silica chains linked to magnesium–aluminium octahedral sheets, with long water channels inside.
It forms in shallow lake, river, marsh and soil settings, favoured by semi-arid conditions with high evaporation and alkaline water rich in magnesium and silica.
Its bristle-like crystals do not swell and have a high specific surface area of about 75 to 400 m²/g.
It is one type of fuller's earth, and in farming serves as a fertilizer carrier and a soil amendment that improves water retention, aeration and nutrient availability.

notes: Assigned to no chapter; own crawled article and mentioned on Clay mineral, Fuller's earth and Montmorillonite.

definition.text: A widespread, poorly crystalline hydrous iron(III) oxyhydroxide mineral that exists only as fine-grained nanoparticles.

facts.text: It forms in soils, waters, aquifers and mining areas, precipitating from oxygenated iron-rich water or through bacterial activity.
Its nanoporous particles give several hundred square metres of surface per gram, which adsorb arsenic, lead, phosphate and humic and fulvic acids.
Metastable, it is a precursor of hematite and goethite, though adsorbed impurities such as silica usually block that change in nature.
Under reducing conditions such as gley soils, often with microbial help, it can turn into green rust (fougerite), which brief contact with air oxidises back to ferrihydrite.

definition.text: A common iron oxide mineral, Fe2O3, widely found in rocks and soils.

facts.text: Clay-sized hematite forms as a secondary mineral during soil weathering and, with goethite and other iron oxides, gives many tropical, ancient or highly weathered soils their red colour.
It grows from ferrihydrite, a metastable precursor of both hematite and goethite.
Its name comes from the Greek for blood; red ochre is clay coloured by 20% to 70% unhydrated hematite.
Older ironstone crusts in Plinthosols contain more hematite and boehmite than plinthite does.

definition.text: A group of sheet silicate minerals whose crystals split easily into thin, elastic plates, a property called perfect basal cleavage.

facts.text: The mica group comprises 37 phyllosilicate minerals; muscovite and the biotite series are common examples.
Its TOT-c structure stacks layers of two tetrahedral sheets bonded to one octahedral sheet, held together only weakly by interlayer cations, hence the cleavage.
In most micas aluminium replaces one in four silicon ions, leaving each layer a negative charge that interlayer sodium, potassium or calcium ions neutralize.
Dioctahedral micas have a gibbsite-like aluminium sheet, while trioctahedral ones have a brucite-like sheet of magnesium or ferrous iron.
Very fine-grained, variable 'clay micas' include illite, which is short of potassium in the interlayer.
Mica is common in igneous and metamorphic rocks and occurs as small flakes in some sedimentary rocks.
Weathering of muscovite yields illite and, with feldspars, kaolin minerals such as dickite.

definition.text: The applied branch of chemistry that studies the structures, properties and reactions of clays and clay minerals.

facts.text: Clay minerals are built of nanometre-scale layers, carry fixed and exchangeable charges, adsorb and intercalate molecules and form stable colloidal dispersions.
Their cation exchange capacity balances the commonest soil cations (Na+, K+, NH4+, Ca2+, Mg2+) and controls pH, directly affecting soil fertility.
Interactions between clay minerals and soil organic substances help fix nutrients and decide whether pesticides and other contaminants are held or leached.
Clay minerals detected on Mars by the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter in 2009 were strong evidence that the planet once had water.

definition.text: Identifying clay minerals by passing X-rays through oriented samples and measuring the spacing of their stacked silicate layers.

facts.text: Ordered atoms in a crystal diffract an X-ray beam at particular angles and intensities, from which the structure is calculated; non-crystalline material can also be recognised.

Randomly oriented powders help little because clays share similar X and Y dimensions; the diagnostic Z dimension is the height of the T-O or T-O-T layer, so samples are oriented to boost basal (00l) reflections.
The Z spacing changes with substitution of the central cations in the sheets and with the presence and size of the interlayer cation.
Layer spacings come from Bragg's law written as l λ = 2d sin θ, so successive 00l peaks are evenly spaced.
Clays give broad peaks while well-crystallized minerals give sharp ones; some peaks broader than others suggest that several clays are present.
Patterns are compared with known samples, such as the Clay Mineral Society's reference collection, because calculated patterns rarely match experiment.
Clays are nearly always mixed with quartz, feldspars, zeolites or carbonates that give intense peaks, so samples are lightly crushed and sieved to remove the harder nonclays.
Of four common mounting methods, the glass slide is fastest but least accurate, while the centrifuged porous plate gives the best patterns, needs most skill, and lets exchangeable cations be swapped.

definition.text: Clay minerals in which layers of two or more clay types are intergrown in one crystal, also called mixed-layer clays; the term does not mean clays physically mixed together.

facts.text: Two-component mixed-layer clays are the most common; those with more than two components are very rare.
A 50/50 mixed-layer clay is easiest to identify, behaving like one clay whose 001 spacing equals the sum of its two components' spacings.
Some regular 50/50 types get their own names, such as dozyite (serpentine/chlorite); a coefficient of variation of d(001) below 0.75% earns a unique name, above it mixed-layer nomenclature applies.
Unequal components stacked at random give aperiodic 'irrational' diffraction patterns, so several analyses are usually needed.

definition.text: A smectite clay mineral in which more than half of the layer charge comes from aluminium replacing silicon in the tetrahedral sheet.

facts.text: It is a dioctahedral smectite, grouped with montmorillonite and nontronite, whereas saponite is trioctahedral.
It is one of the clay minerals that give soils shrink–swell behaviour, along with smectite, montmorillonite, illite and vermiculite.

definition.text: The net negative charge on a clay mineral layer created when ions of lower charge, such as Al3+, replace Si4+, which interlayer cations balance.

facts.text: In nontronite usually more than 60% of the layer charge sits in the tetrahedral sheet, and it is generally balanced by Ca2+ or Mg2+.
Beidellite is defined by having more than 50% of its charge in the tetrahedral sheet.
In the manganese oxide birnessite, cations and water held between layers offset the layer charge, giving the mineral a cation-exchange capacity.
The presence and size of the charge-balancing interlayer cation changes the layer spacing measured by X-ray diffraction.

definition.text: A mixture in which microscopically small insoluble particles are dispersed throughout another substance.

facts.text: A colloid has a dispersed phase, the suspended particles, and a continuous phase, the medium they are suspended in.
IUPAC defines colloidal particles as having at least one dimension roughly between 1 nanometre and 1 micrometre, limits it says are not rigid.
Some colloids look translucent because their particles scatter light, the Tyndall effect.

Particles interact through excluded-volume repulsion, electrostatic attraction or repulsion, always-present short-range van der Waals attraction, steric repulsion from adsorbed polymers and depletion forces.
In soil, the colloidal fraction is tiny clay and humus particles under 1 μm across, whose positive or negative charges vary with soil pH.
Environmental colloids include inorganic particles such as clays, silicates and iron oxy-hydroxides, and organic ones such as humic and fulvic substances.
The study began with Francesco Selmi in 1845; Thomas Graham coined the word colloid in 1861.

definition.text: The ability of colloidal particles to stay suspended instead of clumping, which depends on the forces between them.

facts.text: A colloid stays stable while the attractive interaction energy between particles is below kT; above that, particles begin to clump.
Clumping is called aggregation, flocculation or coagulation; coagulation may mean permanent aggregation and flocculation a reversible one that forms a floc.
Aggregation leads to sedimentation or creaming, ending the suspension.
Particles are stabilized electrostatically, by the like charges of their double layers of counterions, or sterically, by adsorbed polymer or surfactant layers.
Adding salt shrinks the double layer, and shifting pH neutralizes surface charge; either removes the repulsion and lets van der Waals forces aggregate the particles.
When the zeta potential falls below about ±5 mV, rapid coagulation tends to follow.
Charged polymer flocculants bridge particles; negatively charged clay particles, for example, flocculate when a positively charged polymer is added.
Concentrated unstable suspensions form viscoelastic colloidal gels, such as bentonite, that flow under shear but hold their shape at rest.

title: Colloid-facilitated contaminant transport

definition.text: The carrying of contaminants by suspended colloidal particles through surface water and through groundwater in fissured rock.

facts.text: Radionuclides and heavy metals readily sorb onto colloids suspended in water.
When heavy metals or radionuclides form pure colloids of their own, such as Tc(OH)4 or U(OH)4, these are called eigencolloids.
Colloids are suspected of carrying plutonium long distances at the Nevada Nuclear Test Site.
Inorganic colloids barely move through compacted bentonite or deep clay, which filter them out by ultrafiltration.

notes: duplicate of Colloid-facilitated transport (solute transport chapter)

definition.text: A quantitative theory of colloid stability that sums van der Waals attraction and electrical double-layer repulsion between charged surfaces in a liquid.

facts.text: The total potential energy between two particles is the sum of attraction and repulsion; both grow as the particles approach.
The energy curve has a deep primary minimum at very close range, an energy barrier further out, and a shallow secondary minimum beyond it.
The barrier must exceed the thermal energy or particles aggregate; its height shows how stable the dispersion is.
Particles trapped in the primary minimum coagulate irreversibly, while those in the secondary minimum are held weakly and easily redispersed.
Derjaguin and Landau proposed it in 1941 and Verwey and Overbeek reached the same result independently in 1948.
It explained how dispersion stability depends on electrolyte ionic strength, which the earlier Levine–Dube theory could not.
Its electrostatic term uses κ, the inverse of the Debye–Hückel screening length, with κ² = 4πλB n for monovalent ions at concentration n.
Forces outside the theory also affect stability, and it cannot describe colloidal crystals forming in dilute, low-salt dispersions.

definition.text: The sticking together of particles dispersed in a liquid into irregular flocs or agglomerates, which destabilizes a colloid.

facts.text: Also called coagulation or flocculation, it is triggered by adding salts or chemicals known as coagulants or flocculants, and can be reversible or irreversible.
Growing agglomerates settle out as sediment, or in concentrated suspensions link into a colloidal gel.
The reverse, peptization, hardly happens spontaneously but can occur under stirring or shear.
Added salt screens double-layer repulsion so van der Waals attraction dominates; the stability ratio W is near one in fast aggregation and very large in a stable suspension.
Each counter-ion charge has a critical coagulation concentration; because particles are often negative, multivalent metal cations are highly effective coagulants.
Polymers can protect particles by steric repulsion, or, when loosely adsorbed, bridge two particles in bridging flocculation.
Aggregation driven only by diffusion is perikinetic; aggregation sped up by shear such as stirring is orthokinetic.
Clusters are mass fractals: fast, diffusion-limited aggregation makes loose clusters (d ≈ 1.8), slow, reaction-limited aggregation compact ones (d ≈ 2.1).

definition.text: The rule that the critical coagulation concentration of an electrolyte varies as the inverse sixth power of the charge of its counter-ion.

facts.text: Critical coagulation concentrations fall steeply with counter-ion charge; for trivalent counter-ions they range from 0.03 to 0.5 × 10⁻³ mol/L.
The rule can be derived from DLVO theory.
Ions of the same charge still differ somewhat, reflecting particle properties or ion affinities for the surface.
Multivalent cations flocculate colloids more efficiently than monovalent ones: AlCl3 > CaCl2 > NaCl.

definition.text: The electrical potential at the slipping plane around a dispersed particle, the boundary between fluid that moves with the particle and fluid that does not.

facts.text: It is usually given in millivolts and written ζ.
It differs from the Stern or surface potential of the double layer, but is often the only way to characterize double-layer properties.
It is a readily measured indicator of dispersion stability: colloids with high zeta potential, positive or negative, are electrically stabilized, while low values lead to coagulation or flocculation.
Magnitudes of 0 to 5 mV give rapid coagulation, 30 to 40 mV moderate stability, 40 to 60 mV good stability and over 61 mV excellent stability.
It is measured by applying an electric field: particles move toward the opposite electrode at a velocity proportional to their zeta potential, tracked by laser Doppler anemometry.
Electrophoresis is used for particles, streaming potential or current for porous bodies and flat surfaces.
The point of zero charge can be found where titration curves and pH–zeta potential curves intersect.

definition.text: Turning a settled precipitate back into a colloid by shaking it with a suitable electrolyte, a peptizing agent, so that the solid particles are suspended again.

facts.text: It is the reverse of flocculation and is also called deflocculation.
Concentrated salt compresses the electrical double layer, which collapses at high ionic strength, so particles coalesce into an easily filtered flocculent precipitate.
Washing such a precipitate with too much deionised water re-expands the double layer, repulsion returns and the precipitate peptizes.
Freshly precipitated aluminium or iron hydroxide is very hard to filter because its fine colloidal particles pass through paper filters.

definition.text: Inorganic compounds of a metal, hydroxide and weakly bound water.

facts.text: Examples include hydrous ferric oxide (HFO), hydrous aluminium oxide (HAO), hydrous cupric oxide and hydrous titanium oxide.
HFO and HAO precipitate in highly porous, poorly crystalline or amorphous forms that make good adsorbents, used for example in water treatment.
Oxidative weathering of rocks can produce HFO and HAO, giving iron and aluminium hydrous oxide clay soils.

title: Iron oxides

definition.text: Compounds of iron and oxygen, together with the related ferric oxyhydroxides such as rust.

facts.text: They contain ferrous iron, ferric iron or both, and are often non-stoichiometric.
Only a few oxides matter at the Earth's surface, chiefly wüstite, magnetite and hematite; Fe2O3 occurs as hematite (α) and maghemite (γ) among other phases.
The oxyhydroxides include goethite (α-FeOOH), akaganéite (β), lepidocrocite (γ), feroxyhyte (δ), ferrihydrite and green rust.
Goethite and lepidocrocite are the commonest forms of iron(III) oxyhydroxide and the most important mineral carriers of iron in soils.
Iron(III) oxyhydroxide ranges from yellow through dark brown to black depending on hydration, particle size and shape, and crystal structure.
Bacteria such as Shewanella oneidensis and Geobacter species use iron oxides as terminal electron acceptors.
Iron(III) oxyhydroxide precipitates from iron(III) solutions at pH 6.5 to 8 and forms readily when iron(II) hydroxide meets air.
Iron oxide-hydroxide binds phosphate in aquarium water treatment, and its nanoparticles have been studied for removing lead from water.

notes: Folds in the Iron(III) oxide-hydroxide page (S:924f6535f091, S:c58501038639, S:25c45313fcfb, S:017f1fba3185, S:f3ce94723e0c, S:5d688df25ce5).

definition.text: An iron oxide-hydroxide mineral, γ-FeO(OH), also called esmeraldite or hydrohematite.

facts.text: Red to reddish brown, it forms when iron-bearing substances rust underwater and is common where primary iron minerals weather.
Its layers of iron(III) oxide octahedra, held by hydrogen bonds through hydroxide layers as in boehmite, are weakly bonded, giving its scaly habit.
In oxidizing conditions green rust generally turns into goethite and lepidocrocite.
First described in 1813 from Moravia, it takes its name from the Greek for scale and fibre.

definition.text: An iron ore made of a variable mixture of hydrated iron(III) oxide-hydroxides.

facts.text: Once thought a single mineral, it is now a field term for a mixture including goethite, lepidocrocite, akaganeite and jarosite, whose exact makeup only X-ray diffraction can settle.
It forms by hydration of hematite and magnetite, oxidation of iron sulfides and weathering of iron-rich minerals, and is often the main iron component of lateritic soils.
Its name comes from Greek words for wet meadow or marshy lake, after its occurrence as bog iron ore.
Its yellowish-brown streak distinguishes it from hematite, with a red streak, and magnetite, with a black one.

definition.text: A ferrimagnetic iron oxide, γ-Fe2O3, with the formula of hematite but the spinel structure of magnetite.

facts.text: It forms by weathering or low-temperature oxidation of iron(II) spinels such as magnetite, or by dehydration of lepidocrocite and ferrihydrite.
It is a widespread brown or yellow pigment in sediments and soils, and also forms where bushfires have magnetised iron minerals.
Heating converts goethite and ferrihydrite to maghemite and raises soil magnetism; maghemite enrichment across a landscape points to fire.
A soil's magnetic susceptibility reflects magnetic iron oxides such as maghemite, a property geoarchaeologists measure.

definition.text: A soft, white, fibrous magnesium silicate clay mineral, Mg4Si6O15(OH)2·6H2O, also known as meerschaum.

facts.text: The fibrous clays form a continuous series from sepiolite, the most magnesium-rich, to palygorskite; sepiolite has wider structural channels.
It occurs as a secondary mineral with serpentine and can precipitate in arid environments.
Soils of South Africa's arid west hold much sepiolite, grading inland to palygorskite; it raises plant-available water in sandy soils, but cemented layers hamper mining.
Sepiolite-cemented material is called sepiocrete, and soils rich in it may be termed sepiolitic or petrosepiolitic.

definition.text: Determining a material's surface area per unit mass, most often by gas adsorption with the BET method.

facts.text: Results depend on the method: the probe molecule's size, the exposed crystal faces and the temperature all change the value obtained.
Calculating it from a particle size distribution needs an assumed particle shape and misses the particles' surface texture.
BET adsorption captures fine structure and deep texture, but results can differ markedly with the substance adsorbed.
Gas permeability through a powder bed is quick and simple but misses much deep surface texture; standards such as ISO 9277 govern measurement.
They occur as minerals, coal combustion products and synthetic materials, often zeolites, and matter technically as structural materials, catalysts and reagents.
Feldspar is a common tectosilicate aluminosilicate of potassium, sodium and calcium cations in a negatively charged network of silicon, aluminium and oxygen.
Soil alumino-silica clays are aluminosilicates with regular crystalline or quasi-crystalline structure, including montmorillonite, illite, vermiculite, chlorite and kaolinite.
Naturally occurring microporous, hydrous aluminosilicate minerals are zeolites; their Si/Al ratio varies, which tunes their properties.

definition.text: Aluminosilicates are materials containing anionic Si-O-Al linkages, with cations such as sodium, potassium or hydrogen balancing the charge.

facts.text: Dispersions are classed by particle size relative to the continuous phase, whether precipitation occurs and Brownian motion; particles big enough to sediment make suspensions, smaller ones colloids and solutions.

Dispersing a solid in a liquid separates agglomerated particles and creates a new interface; it is driven by molecular diffusion and convection, with convection dominating in turbulent flow and diffusion where there is little turbulence.
Above a critical concentration, which depends on particle size and interfacial tension, some liquid dispersions turn into gels or solids.

definition.text: A dispersion is a system in which particles of one material are distributed in a continuous phase of another.

title: Flocculation

facts.text: In colloid chemistry flocculation is when colloidal particles leave suspension as floc or flake; unlike precipitation they were first merely suspended in a stable dispersion.
The IUPAC definition is contact and adhesion that makes larger clusters; agglomeration of this kind is reversible, so the particles can be dispersed again.
In dispersed clay slurries, flocs form once agitation stops because negative face charges attract positive edge charges.
Flocculation of soil colloids is tied to freshwater quality: highly dispersible colloids make water turbid and adsorb nutrients that drive eutrophication.
The forces involved include van der Waals forces, electrostatic forces and hydrogen bonding.
It is the opposite of dispersion, in which particles are held apart; the balance between them is set mainly by soil pH, electrical conductivity and sodium content.
Clay plates flocculate when their slightly positive edges stick to the negative faces of other plates; sodium displacing polyvalent cations weakens this and deflocculates the clay.
Floccules become lasting aggregates only once cementing agents stabilize them.

notes: The Flocculation article (a frame candidate) was not crawled, so the entry is anchored on a section.

title: Coagulation and flocculation in water treatment

facts.text: Alum is the most common coagulant; gentle mixing then speeds particle collisions so destabilized particles enmesh in larger precipitates, depending on mixing shear, intensity, time and pH.
A jar test chooses the flocculant and dose by rapid mixing, slow mixing and sedimentation in beakers with paddle mixers.

Drinking-water treatment typically runs grates, coagulation, flocculation, sedimentation, granular filtration and disinfection; chitosan is an increasingly popular biodegradable flocculant that binds heavy metals and organic pollutants.

definition.text: Coagulation destabilizes charged particles with an added coagulant, and flocculation then gathers them into settleable clusters.

facts.text: Its TOT-c structure has tetrahedral-octahedral-tetrahedral layers bonded by potassium cations; strong bonds within layers and weak ones between them give perfect basal cleavage into thin elastic sheets.
It is the most common mica, found in granites, pegmatites, gneisses and schists, and as an alteration product of feldspar.
Biotite is almost always much darker, chlorite is green with inelastic sheets, and pyrophyllite and talc are softer and greasy.
Up to 10% of its potassium may be replaced by sodium, and phengite has more silicon than aluminium with Mg or Fe balancing charge.

definition.text: Muscovite, also called common mica or potash mica, is a hydrated phyllosilicate of aluminium and potassium, KAl2(AlSi3O10)(OH)2.
A weak, distance-dependent attraction between atoms or molecules that is not a chemical bond.

facts.text: It arises from a transient shift in electron density that creates a short-lived charge, which a nearby atom is attracted to or repelled by.
The force is repulsive at very short range, zero at an equilibrium distance of 0.3 to 0.5 nm for single atoms, and attractive beyond it; past 1.0 nm it falls off roughly as the 7th power of distance.

It combines London dispersion forces, Debye forces between permanent and induced dipoles, and Keesom forces between permanent dipoles; induction and dispersion are always attractive, while the electrostatic part can attract or repel depending on orientation.
Strength rises with polarizability: pairwise energy is 0.06 kJ/mol between H atoms in H2 molecules, 0.44 kJ/mol between O atoms in O2, and 2.35 kJ/mol between xenon atoms.
The forces are additive, cannot be saturated and have no directional character, so many weak contacts can add up to strong attraction.

For very small particles such as fine dry powders, van der Waals attraction dominates over gravity and drag, so such powders are cohesive; free flow generally needs particles larger than about 250 micrometres.
In soils, organic contaminants can be held in organic matter by weak van der Waals interactions, and physisorption is the weak van der Waals form of adsorption.

definition.text: The change in direction of X-ray beams by elastic scattering from the electrons around atoms, giving a diffraction pattern.

facts.text: A regular array of atoms scatters X-rays as secondary spherical waves that cancel in most directions but add up in a few specific ones; the Bragg model explains these as reflections from evenly spaced sheets in the crystal.
Scattering is set by electron density; the heavy nuclei contribute negligibly.

Laboratory sources are tubes whose electrons, accelerated through about 50 kV, hit a metal plate; copper is most common because it cools easily and gives strong K-alpha and K-beta lines. Synchrotrons are far brighter.
Where single crystals are unavailable, powder diffraction gives less detailed information; Max von Laue's 1912 observation of diffraction confirmed that X-rays are electromagnetic radiation.
Neutrons scatter from nuclei and so reveal light atoms such as hydrogen, which is nearly invisible to X-rays; electrons scatter 1000 or more times more strongly than X-rays.
